title: A dusty beauty
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 66 (NGC 3627), imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: Messier 66, NGC 3627 · constellation Leo · about 35 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Large-scale dust lanes wind through this spiral galaxy, which has a well-developed central bulge and many regions of warm hydrogen gas scattered across its disc. This is NGC 3627, also known as Messier 66, in the constellation Leo, the Lion, imaged with ESO's Very Large Telescope.

Radiation from clusters of newborn stars is ionizing these hydrogen regions, and very active star formation is probably also going on in the galaxy's nuclear regions. M66 is the largest member of the Leo Triplet, alongside M 65 and NGC 3628, all three about 35 million light-years away.

Its spiral arms look distorted and lifted above the galaxy's main plane. The lopsided look is probably the result of gravitational tugging by the other two galaxies. The galaxy's number comes from its place as the 66th object in Charles Messier's famous catalog of nebulae.
scale: The source lists a distance of 35 million light years, so the light in this picture set out roughly 35 million years ago.

understand.summary: FORS1 and FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope recorded blue (B), visual (V) and red (R) exposures. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint dust lanes and gas regions beyond what the eye would see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The photo was made with the FORS1 and FORS2 instruments on the VLT's MELIPAL and YEPUN telescopes, combining three exposures in different wavebands. Charles Messier, the French astronomer who compiled the catalog, lived from 1730 to 1817.
alt: A spiral galaxy with a well-developed central bulge, prominent dust lanes and glowing gas regions across its disc.
